topics.name: Battle of Chancellorsville
topics.kicker: Lee’s great 1863 victory over Hooker · Stonewall Jackson shot by his own men
topics.briefing: In May 1863, Robert E. Lee faced a Union army more than twice the size of his own near a crossroads in the Virginia woods called Chancellorsville. Lee boldly split his army and sent Stonewall Jackson on a secret march around the Union flank, and the surprise attack sent Joseph Hooker’s army reeling. But that night, Jackson was accidentally shot by his own men, and he died eight days later.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of Chancellorsville (do not accept “Battle of the Wilderness” or “Fredericksburg”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On the night of May 2, 1863, during this battle, soldiers of the 18th North Carolina Infantry fired into a group of riders returning from a scouting trip in the dark, mistaking them for Union cavalry.
tossups.r: That volley badly wounded their own general, Stonewall Jackson. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle in Virginia, a victory for Robert E. Lee.

tossups.p: Ernest Hemingway took the title of his 1950 novel _Across the River and into the Trees_ from the last words of a general who was wounded in this battle. That general said, “Let us cross over the river and rest under the shade of the trees.”
tossups.r: That general, Stonewall Jackson, died of pneumonia eight days after he was shot by his own men. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle won by Robert E. Lee.

tossups.p: On the night of May 1, 1863, two generals sat on empty cracker boxes and planned a daring march after cavalry under Fitzhugh Lee found that the Union right flank was “in the air,” protected by no river or hill.
tossups.r: The next day, Stonewall Jackson’s men marched around that flank and attacked. For 10 points, name this battle in which Robert E. Lee defeated Joseph Hooker.

tossups.p: During this battle, a cannonball struck a porch pillar that a Union commander was leaning against at a brick house, leaving him dazed. Earlier that morning, May 3, he had ordered his troops to give up Hazel Grove, a clearing where Confederate cannons soon set up.
tossups.r: That commander was Joseph Hooker. For 10 points, name this battle in Virginia, Robert E. Lee’s greatest victory.

tossups.p: While the main armies fought to the west during this battle, John Sedgwick’s Union corps captured Marye’s Heights at Fredericksburg, but it was stopped at Salem Church and had to retreat across the Rappahannock River.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle where Stonewall Jackson was accidentally shot by his own troops, a loss Lee compared to losing his own right arm.

tossups.p: Before this battle, the Union commander sent most of his cavalry under George Stoneman on a raid toward Richmond, which left him with little information about the enemy’s movements.
tossups.r: That commander, Joseph Hooker, was then surprised by Stonewall Jackson’s flank attack. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle in Virginia.

tossups.p: Before this battle, a Union general reportedly boasted that his plans were perfect and “may God have mercy on General Lee, for I will have none.” That general marched most of his army across the Rappahannock and Rapidan Rivers to get behind Lee, then pulled back to defend.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle in which Joseph Hooker lost to Robert E. Lee and Stonewall Jackson.

tossups.p: According to the journalist Noah Brooks, Abraham Lincoln paced the room after hearing the news of this battle, crying out, “My God! My God! What will the country say?” The defeated Union army had outnumbered its enemy by more than two to one.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1863 Union defeat, in which Stonewall Jackson was mortally wounded by his own men.

tossups.p: Cavalry general Jeb Stuart temporarily led an infantry corps on May 3, 1863, during this battle, after its commander was wounded and the next general in line, A. P. Hill, was also hurt.
tossups.r: The wounded commander was Stonewall Jackson, who died on May 10. For 10 points, name this battle in which Robert E. Lee defeated Joseph Hooker.

tossups.p: The winning general in this battle fought without James Longstreet, who had taken two divisions to gather supplies near Suffolk in southeastern Virginia. Even so, that general split his outnumbered army twice during this battle and won.
tossups.r: That general was Robert E. Lee. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle where Lee beat Joseph Hooker.

tossups.p: Historians usually identify this battle as the one that Stephen Crane’s novel _The Red Badge of Courage_ never names, in which the young soldier Henry Fleming runs from the fighting and later returns to his regiment.
tossups.r: In real life, this battle was a victory for Robert E. Lee, though Stonewall Jackson was shot by his own men. For 10 points, name this 1863 battle.

tossups.p: The losing general in this battle disliked his nickname, “Fighting Joe,” which came from a newspaper headline that left out a dash. Months before this battle, Abraham Lincoln’s letter giving him command warned, “What I now ask of you is military success, and I will risk the dictatorship.”
tossups.r: That general was Joseph Hooker. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle in which Hooker lost to Robert E. Lee.

tossups.p: Late on the afternoon of May 2, 1863, during this battle, deer and rabbits burst out of the woods toward Union soldiers, many of whom were cooking supper. Moments later, thousands of enemy troops came charging out of the trees behind the animals.
tossups.r: That surprise attack by Stonewall Jackson routed Oliver O. Howard’s XI Corps. For 10 points, name this battle, Robert E. Lee’s greatest victory.

tossups.p: This battle’s site is one of four battlefields preserved in the Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania National Military Park. It was named for a large brick house and inn at a crossroads in a scrubby forest called the Wilderness, not for a town.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle in Virginia, where Robert E. Lee defeated Joseph Hooker.

tossups.p: Historians often call this battle Robert E. Lee’s “perfect battle,” though he lost more than one-fifth of his army in it. Afterward, Lee marched north toward Pennsylvania, and George Meade replaced the losing Union commander just days before the armies met again.
tossups.r: That next meeting came at Gettysburg. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle where Stonewall Jackson was mortally wounded.

Jackson’s attack late on May 2 routed Oliver O. Howard’s Union XI Corps

Usually identified as the unnamed battle in Stephen Crane’s _The Red Badge of Courage_

Ernest Hemingway’s novel _Across the River and into the Trees_ (1950) takes its title from Jackson’s last words
k: across the river and into the trees

Cavalry leader Jeb Stuart took over Jackson’s corps on May 3 after A. P. Hill was also wounded

trap.title: Chancellorsville or the Wilderness?
trap.body: Chancellorsville (May 1863) and the Battle of the Wilderness (May 1864) were fought in the same tangled Virginia forest, a year apart. Chancellorsville was Lee’s win over Joseph Hooker, where Stonewall Jackson was shot; the Wilderness was Lee against Ulysses S. Grant. The first Battle of Fredericksburg (December 1862) was fought just a few miles east, and Gettysburg came two months after Chancellorsville.
trap.fix: Hooker, Jackson’s flank march, and Jackson’s death mean Chancellorsville. Grant and 1864 mean the Wilderness; Ambrose Burnside’s failed charges in December 1862 mean Fredericksburg.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of Chancellorsville (do not accept “Battle of the Wilderness” or “Fredericksburg”)

topics.name: Battle of Iwo Jima
topics.kicker: 1945 Marine battle south of Japan · Flag raising on Mount Suribachi
topics.briefing: Iwo Jima, a tiny volcanic island south of Japan that Japan renamed Iōtō in 2007, is covered in black sand and smells of sulfur. In February 1945, U.S. Marines landed to capture its airfields, and on the fifth day Joe Rosenthal photographed six men raising an American flag on Mount Suribachi, one of the most famous photos ever taken. The battle lasted more than a month; nearly 7,000 Americans and almost all of about 21,000 Japanese defenders died.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of Iwo Jima (or Operation Detachment; accept Iōtō; prompt on Mount Suribachi; do not accept “Okinawa”)
reject: raising the flag on iwo jima

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Staff Sergeant Louis Lowery of _Leatherneck_ magazine photographed an earlier, smaller version of this battle’s most famous moment, but his pictures were overshadowed by ones taken a few hours later on the same summit.
tossups.r: Those later pictures, by Joe Rosenthal, show Marines raising a large flag on Mount Suribachi. For 10 points, name this February 1945 battle.

tossups.p: Marine cameraman Bill Genaust shot color film of this battle’s most famous moment while standing just a few feet from a photographer whose still picture of it became famous. Genaust was killed in the fighting days later, and his body was never found.
tossups.r: That photographer, Joe Rosenthal, won a Pulitzer Prize for his picture of a flag raising on Mount Suribachi. For 10 points, name this February 1945 battle.

tossups.p: Navy Secretary James Forrestal came ashore during this battle with Lieutenant General Holland Smith and reportedly told him that a sight on a nearby mountaintop meant “a Marine Corps for the next five hundred years.”
tossups.r: That sight was a U.S. flag flying over Mount Suribachi. For 10 points, name this 1945 battle on a volcanic island south of Japan.

tossups.p: Sculptor Felix de Weldon worked for years to turn a photograph from this battle into a huge bronze statue, which was dedicated in Arlington, Virginia, on November 10, 1954, the Marine Corps’ birthday. Its base quotes Admiral Chester Nimitz: “Uncommon valor was a common virtue.”
tossups.r: That statue, the Marine Corps War Memorial, shows Marines raising a flag on Mount Suribachi. For 10 points, name this 1945 battle.

tossups.p: Gunnery Sergeant John Basilone, who had already won the Medal of Honor at Guadalcanal, was killed on the first day of this battle, February 19, 1945, while leading his men inland from the beach.
tossups.r: Four days later, Marines raised a flag atop Mount Suribachi. For 10 points, name this battle on an island south of Japan.

tossups.p: Johnny Cash recorded a 1964 ballad about Ira Hayes, a Pima [“PEE-muh”] Marine from Arizona who came home a hero after this battle but struggled for the rest of his short life.
tossups.r: Hayes was one of the men in Joe Rosenthal’s photo of a flag raising in this battle. For 10 points, name this 1945 battle.

tossups.p: James Bradley’s book _Flags of Our Fathers_ is about his father, a Navy medical corpsman long believed to appear in a famous photo from this battle. Clint Eastwood turned that book into a 2006 film and made a companion film the same year about the Japanese defenders.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle, where Marines raised the U.S. flag on Mount Suribachi in February 1945.

tossups.p: Japanese general Tadamichi Kuribayashi [“koo-ree-bah-YAH-shee”] had his troops dig miles of tunnels and hidden bunkers before this battle, and he ordered them not to waste their lives in mass charges. Nearly all of his roughly 21,000 men died.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1945 battle in which U.S. Marines raised a flag on Mount Suribachi.

tossups.p: After this battle, P-51 Mustang fighters flying from its island escorted B-29 bombers on raids over Japan, and thousands of crewmen in damaged B-29s made emergency landings on its airfields.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this February 1945 battle, famous for a photo of Marines raising a flag on Mount Suribachi.

tossups.p: A Marine signal officer said that the Marines would never have taken this battle’s island without the Navajo code talkers; six of them sent more than 800 messages without an error during its first two days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1945 battle in which Marines raised a flag on Mount Suribachi.

tossups.p: Twenty-seven Medals of Honor were awarded for actions in this battle, and Admiral Chester Nimitz said that among the Americans who served there, “uncommon valor was a common virtue.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle that began on February 19, 1945, and is remembered for a flag raising on Mount Suribachi.

tossups.p: This battle’s island is part of Japan’s Volcano Islands, about 750 miles south of Tokyo, and its name means “Sulfur Island.” Its soft black volcanic sand made it hard for Marines to dig foxholes or move vehicles off the beaches.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this February 1945 battle, famous for a photo of Marines raising a flag on Mount Suribachi.

tossups.p: Marine commanders asked for ten days of naval shelling before this battle but received only three, so most of the enemy’s hidden guns survived to fire on the landing beaches.
tossups.r: Marines came ashore on February 19, 1945. For 10 points, name this battle, where a famous photo showed Marines raising a flag.

tossups.p: Major General Harry Schmidt led the 3rd, 4th, and 5th Marine Divisions of the V Amphibious Corps in this battle, which lasted more than a month on an island of only about eight square miles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle, fought from February to March 1945, whose flag raising inspired the Marine Corps War Memorial.

tossups.p: John Wayne earned an Oscar nomination for playing a tough sergeant in a 1949 film about this battle, in which three men then believed to be in a famous photograph from it made brief appearances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this February 1945 battle, where Marines raised a flag on Mount Suribachi.

clues.t: Joe Rosenthal’s photo shows six Marines raising a U.S. flag on Mount Suribachi (February 23, 1945)
Fought February 19–March 26, 1945, on a small volcanic island south of Japan
One of the deadliest battles in U.S. Marine Corps history
The Marine Corps War Memorial in Arlington, Virginia, is based on the flag-raising photo
The U.S. wanted its airfields as an emergency landing place for B-29 bombers flying to and from Japan
Japanese commander Tadamichi Kuribayashi had his men dig tunnels and bunkers instead of defending the beaches
Admiral Chester Nimitz: “Uncommon valor was a common virtue”
Ira Hayes, a Pima Marine from Arizona, was one of the six men in Rosenthal’s photo
Nearly 7,000 Americans were killed, and almost all of the roughly 21,000 Japanese defenders died
Rosenthal’s photo won the 1945 Pulitzer Prize for Photography
The island’s name means “Sulfur Island”; its black volcanic sand made digging and driving hard
Navajo code talkers sent hundreds of messages; an officer said the Marines could not have won without them
Three of the six men in Rosenthal’s photo were killed later in the battle
Louis Lowery of _Leatherneck_ magazine photographed the first, smaller flag on Suribachi; the larger second flag went up hours later
Marine cameraman Bill Genaust filmed the second flag raising in color, a few feet from Rosenthal
Navy Secretary James Forrestal reportedly said the flag on Suribachi meant “a Marine Corps for the next five hundred years”
Felix de Weldon sculpted the Marine Corps War Memorial, dedicated November 10, 1954, the Marine Corps’ birthday
Twenty-seven Medals of Honor were awarded for actions there
John Basilone, a Medal of Honor hero of Guadalcanal, was killed on the first day
Johnny Cash recorded “The Ballad of Ira Hayes” (1964) about the Pima Marine’s hard life after the war
James Bradley’s _Flags of Our Fathers_ became a 2006 Clint Eastwood film; Eastwood also made a companion film from the Japanese side
After the battle, P-51 Mustangs flying from the island escorted B-29s on raids over Japan
Part of Japan’s Volcano Islands, about 750 miles south of Tokyo; in 1945 the island covered only about 8 square miles
Marine commanders asked for ten days of naval shelling before the landing but got only three
Harry Schmidt’s V Amphibious Corps landed the 3rd, 4th, and 5th Marine Divisions; Holland Smith commanded all the expeditionary troops
John Wayne was nominated for an Oscar for a 1949 film about the battle

trap.title: Iwo Jima or Okinawa?
trap.body: The two biggest Marine battles of 1945 are easy to mix up. Iwo Jima (February–March 1945) was a small volcanic island captured for its airfields, with the famous flag raising on Mount Suribachi. Okinawa (April–June 1945) was a much larger island and the last major battle of the Pacific war, where kamikaze planes attacked U.S. ships.
trap.fix: Suribachi, Rosenthal’s photo, Kuribayashi, black volcanic sand, and B-29 emergency landings mean Iwo Jima; kamikazes and an April 1945 invasion mean Okinawa. Saying “Mount Suribachi” alone earns only a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of Iwo Jima (or Operation Detachment; accept Iōtō; prompt on Mount Suribachi; do not accept “Okinawa”)

topics.name: Battles of Lexington and Concord
topics.kicker: First battles of the Revolution, 1775 · “The shot heard round the world”
topics.briefing: On the night of April 18, 1775, Paul Revere and William Dawes rode out of Boston to warn that British troops were marching to seize the colonists’ gunpowder and weapons. At dawn the next day, shots rang out on the town green at Lexington, and later that morning militiamen drove the British back at Concord’s North Bridge, firing Emerson’s famous “shot heard round the world.” The redcoats retreated to Boston under fire, and the American Revolution had begun.
topics.answerHtml: Battles of Lexington and Concord (accept either underlined part; prompt on North Bridge; do not accept “Bunker Hill”)
accept: the battles of lexington and concord

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Prince Estabrook, an enslaved Black man serving in Captain John Parker’s militia company, was wounded in the first clash of this pair of battles. That clash took place around sunrise on a town green, where eight militiamen were killed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these battles of April 19, 1775, that began the American Revolution.

tossups.p: Captain Isaac Davis of Acton was killed leading his company toward a bridge during this pair of battles, and Major John Buttrick then ordered the militia to return fire. The British soldiers guarding the bridge soon fell back toward the town.
tossups.r: Ralph Waldo Emerson called that volley “the shot heard round the world.” For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles.

tossups.p: Daniel Chester French, who later designed the seated statue in the Lincoln Memorial, made his first major work, a farmer-soldier holding a musket beside a plow, for the 100th anniversary of this pair of battles in 1875.
tossups.r: That statue, _The Minute Man_, stands near the North Bridge. For 10 points, name these battles that began the Revolution in April 1775.

tossups.p: At the dedication of a battle monument on July 4, 1837, townspeople sang a hymn by a local writer whose grandfather had been the town’s minister in 1775. That hymn says the “embattled farmers” stood by “the rude bridge that arched the flood.”
tossups.r: Its writer, Ralph Waldo Emerson, called their first volley “the shot heard round the world.” For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles.

tossups.p: Lord Hugh Percy led about 1,000 British reinforcements out of Boston during this pair of battles, bringing cannons to rescue an exhausted column that was retreating under fire. Percy’s men met that column in the early afternoon, near the site of the morning’s first shots.
tossups.r: Afterward, militiamen surrounded Boston, beginning a long siege. For 10 points, name these battles of April 19, 1775, the first fighting of the American Revolution.

tossups.p: On the night before this pair of battles, two men quietly rowed a silversmith across the Charles River, past the British warship HMS _Somerset_. In Charlestown, the silversmith borrowed a horse and rode off to spread the alarm.
tossups.r: That rider was Paul Revere, sent by Dr. Joseph Warren. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles that started the American Revolution.

tossups.p: Sexton Robert Newman climbed a church steeple on the night before this pair of battles to hang a signal meant for patriots across the river in Charlestown, in case the man who arranged it was caught.
tossups.r: That signal was two lanterns in Boston’s Old North Church, meaning the British were crossing by water. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles.

tossups.p: Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith commanded the British troops sent out during this pair of battles, and Major John Pitcairn of the Royal Marines led the advance companies that met the first militiamen.
tossups.r: General Thomas Gage had sent those troops to seize colonial weapons and gunpowder. For 10 points, name these battles of April 19, 1775.

tossups.p: Words carved on a boulder at the site of this pair of battles’ first clash, credited to a militia captain, read: “Stand your ground. Don’t fire unless fired upon, but if they mean to have a war, let it begin here.”
tossups.r: That captain was John Parker. For 10 points, name these battles of April 19, 1775, in which minutemen faced British redcoats.

tossups.p: British soldiers searched Colonel James Barrett’s farm for hidden cannons during this pair of battles. When smoke rose from the town where soldiers were burning captured supplies, militiamen on a nearby hill feared the town was on fire and marched toward a bridge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles in Massachusetts, where Emerson’s “shot heard round the world” was fired.

tossups.p: During the night before this pair of battles, a British patrol captured a famous rider near the town of Lincoln, but Samuel Prescott, a young doctor riding with him, jumped his horse over a stone wall and escaped.
tossups.r: Prescott carried the alarm on to the second town, which Paul Revere never reached. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles.

tossups.p: Samuel Adams and John Hancock were staying at minister Jonas Clarke’s house when riders arrived around midnight to warn them, hours before this pair of battles began. One rider had taken the long way out of Boston, over the narrow neck of land, while the other crossed the river by boat.
tossups.r: Those riders were Paul Revere and William Dawes. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles that began the Revolutionary War.

tossups.p: Fighting broke out again at Meriam’s Corner during this pair of battles, as militiamen from many towns fired from behind stone walls, trees, and houses at a column marching back toward Boston.
tossups.r: By nightfall, more than 70 British soldiers and about 50 colonists had been killed. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles.

tossups.p: Massachusetts and Maine honor this pair of battles with a state holiday on the third Monday in April, the same day the Boston Marathon is run. Reenactors gather on a town green at dawn that day to recreate the first shots.
tossups.r: That holiday is Patriots’ Day. For 10 points, name these battles fought on April 19, 1775.

tossups.p: Historians say a famous rider before this pair of battles probably warned that “the Regulars are coming out,” not that “the British are coming,” since most colonists still thought of themselves as British. A Henry Wadsworth Longfellow poem later made that rider a national hero.
tossups.r: That rider was Paul Revere. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles that began the American Revolution.

clues.t: Fought April 19, 1775, in Massachusetts: the first battles of the American Revolution
Ralph Waldo Emerson called the first volley at the North Bridge “the shot heard round the world”
Paul Revere and William Dawes rode out the night before to warn that British troops were coming
Colonial militiamen called minutemen fought British regulars (redcoats)
Two lanterns in Boston’s Old North Church meant the British were crossing by water (“one if by land, and two if by sea”)
General Thomas Gage sent about 700 soldiers to seize colonial weapons and gunpowder
Captain John Parker’s militia faced the British on a town green at dawn; eight militiamen were killed
Militiamen fired from behind stone walls and trees as the British marched back to Boston
Revere was captured on the way; Samuel Prescott escaped and carried the warning on
Remembered each April on Patriots’ Day, the day of the Boston Marathon
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s poem “Paul Revere’s Ride” made the ride famous
The riders warned Samuel Adams and John Hancock, who were staying at minister Jonas Clarke’s house
Afterward, thousands of militiamen surrounded Boston, starting the Siege of Boston; Bunker Hill came two months later
Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith led the British column; Major John Pitcairn of the Royal Marines led the advance companies
Boulder inscription credited to Parker: “Stand your ground. Don’t fire unless fired upon, but if they mean to have a war, let it begin here”
Historians say Revere probably warned that “the Regulars are coming out,” not “the British are coming”
Captain Isaac Davis of Acton was killed near the bridge; Major John Buttrick ordered the militia to return fire
Daniel Chester French’s statue _The Minute Man_ (1875) stands by the North Bridge
Emerson’s hymn was sung at the dedication of a battle monument on July 4, 1837; it praises the “embattled farmers”
Sexton Robert Newman hung the lanterns; the signal was meant for patriots in Charlestown, not for Revere
Revere was rowed across the Charles River past the British warship HMS _Somerset_, then borrowed a horse
British soldiers searched Colonel James Barrett’s farm; smoke from burning supplies made militiamen think the town was on fire
Lord Hugh Percy’s roughly 1,000 reinforcements, with cannons, rescued the retreating British column
Prince Estabrook, an enslaved Black militiaman, was wounded in the first clash
Fighting broke out again at Meriam’s Corner as the British began their march back
Dr. Joseph Warren, later killed at Bunker Hill, sent Revere and Dawes on their rides
By nightfall, more than 70 British soldiers and about 50 colonists had been killed

trap.title: Not Bunker Hill!
trap.body: These battles happened in two towns on one day, April 19, 1775: the first shots came at dawn on the town green in Lexington, and Emerson’s “shot heard round the world” came later that morning at the North Bridge in Concord. Bunker Hill was a separate, bigger battle two months later, in June 1775. And Paul Revere never reached Concord: a British patrol captured him, and Samuel Prescott carried the warning the rest of the way.
trap.fix: Revere and Dawes, the two lanterns, John Parker, the North Bridge, and Patriots’ Day mean Lexington and Concord. “The whites of their eyes,” Breed’s Hill, and William Howe mean Bunker Hill. This answer line accepts either town alone.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battles of Lexington and Concord (accept either underlined part; prompt on North Bridge; do not accept “Bunker Hill”)

topics.name: Battle of San Jacinto
topics.kicker: Sam Houston’s 18-minute victory, 1836 · Won independence for Texas
topics.briefing: On the afternoon of April 21, 1836, Sam Houston’s ragged Texian army charged across an open field into Santa Anna’s Mexican camp, shouting “Remember the Alamo! Remember Goliad!” The surprise attack was over in about 18 minutes. The next day, Texians captured Santa Anna, who was hiding in a common soldier’s clothes, and Texas won its independence from Mexico.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of San Jacinto (prompt on Texas Revolution; do not accept “Alamo” or “Goliad”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Shortly before this battle, scout Erastus “Deaf” Smith and his men destroyed Vince’s Bridge, cutting off a route that either army might have used to escape or to bring in more troops.
tossups.r: Hours later, Sam Houston’s army attacked and defeated Santa Anna. For 10 points, name this April 21, 1836, battle that won Texas its independence.

tossups.p: As the Texian army advanced in this battle, a fife and drum played a popular love song, “Will You Come to the Bower?” A low rise in the prairie hid the advancing soldiers until they were close to the enemy camp.
tossups.r: Shouting “Remember the Alamo!” they routed Santa Anna’s army in about 18 minutes. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle.

tossups.p: A private named Mirabeau Lamar [“MEER-uh-boh luh-MAR”] rescued Secretary of War Thomas Rusk during a skirmish the day before this battle, and he was promoted to colonel to lead the cavalry in it. Lamar later became the second president of the Republic of Texas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna on April 21, 1836.

tossups.p: Juan Seguín [“seh-GEEN”], who later served as mayor of San Antonio, led a company of Tejano soldiers on the Texian side in this battle. Weeks earlier, he had left the Alamo as a messenger seeking help.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1836 battle where Sam Houston’s army defeated Santa Anna and won independence for Texas.

tossups.p: William Henry Huddle’s 1886 painting of the day after this battle, which hangs in the Texas Capitol, shows a wounded general lying under an oak tree as a captured enemy leader is brought before him.
tossups.r: That general was Sam Houston. For 10 points, name this April 1836 battle where Houston defeated Santa Anna.

tossups.p: On the morning of this battle, General Martín Perfecto de Cos [“KOHSS”] arrived with about 500 Mexican reinforcements, many of them tired from a long march. That afternoon, the Texians attacked the enlarged camp.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which Sam Houston’s army defeated Santa Anna in about 18 minutes.

tossups.p: Citizens of Cincinnati, Ohio, paid for two small cannons that were shipped to the Texian army before this battle. Those cannons, nicknamed the “Twin Sisters,” fired on the enemy during this battle, and what became of them after the Civil War is a mystery.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this April 21, 1836, battle where Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna and won Texas its independence.

tossups.p: Starting in 1948, the battleship USS _Texas_ was docked for decades beside the site of this battle, near a 567-foot monument topped by a giant star. That monument, finished in 1939, is taller than the Washington Monument.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1836 battle near present-day Houston, where Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna.

tossups.p: A legend that historians doubt claims that Emily West, a free Black woman in the Mexican camp, distracted the enemy general just before this battle and inspired the song “The Yellow Rose of Texas.”
tossups.r: In this battle, Sam Houston’s army shouted “Remember the Alamo!” For 10 points, name this April 1836 battle that ended the Texas Revolution.

tossups.p: After this battle, Vicente Filisola [“fee-lee-SOH-lah”] led most of the remaining Mexican army back toward the Rio Grande, obeying orders sent by his captured commander. Filisola, an Italian-born general, had been second-in-command of the Mexican army in Texas.
tossups.r: That commander, Santa Anna, later signed the Treaties of Velasco [“veh-LAHS-koh”]. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle that won independence for Texas.

tossups.p: Before this battle, the winning army spent about two weeks drilling at Groce’s plantation on the Brazos River, while frightened settlers fled east in the panic called the “Runaway Scrape.” Some of its officers grumbled that their commander would never stand and fight.
tossups.r: Sam Houston then turned and attacked Santa Anna. For 10 points, name this April 21, 1836, battle.

tossups.p: The winning general in this battle had a horse shot out from under him and was wounded in the ankle by a musket ball, but he stayed in command until the fighting ended. Weeks later, he sailed to New Orleans for treatment.
tossups.r: That general was Sam Houston. For 10 points, name this battle where Houston’s army defeated Santa Anna in about 18 minutes.

tossups.p: Months after this battle, the losing general traveled to Washington, D.C., where he met President Andrew Jackson in January 1837. As a prisoner, he had signed treaties promising to pull his troops back beyond the Rio Grande.
tossups.r: Texians had captured that general, Santa Anna, the day after this battle. For 10 points, name this April 1836 battle.

tossups.p: Augustus and John Allen founded a town on Buffalo Bayou months after this battle and named it for the battle’s winning general, who soon became the first elected president of the Republic of Texas.
tossups.r: That general was Sam Houston. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle where Houston defeated Santa Anna.

tossups.p: This battle took place on a plain where Buffalo Bayou meets a river, near present-day La Porte, Texas. The attack came late in the afternoon, catching the enemy camp off guard while many soldiers rested.
tossups.r: The fighting lasted about 18 minutes. For 10 points, name this April 21, 1836, battle that won independence for Texas.

trap.title: Battle cry, not answer
trap.body: Tossups about this battle often mention the Alamo and Goliad, because Texian soldiers shouted “Remember the Alamo! Remember Goliad!” as they charged. A player who hears “Alamo” and blurts it out loses the question: the Alamo (February–March 1836) and Goliad (March 1836) were Texian defeats, while this battle on April 21, 1836, was the victory that won independence.
trap.fix: Sam Houston’s surprise attack, an 18-minute battle, the Twin Sisters cannons, and Santa Anna’s capture the next day mean San Jacinto. “Remember the Alamo” is the battle cry shouted here, not the answer.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of San Jacinto (prompt on Texas Revolution; do not accept “Alamo” or “Goliad”)
